summary: Defines how to carry JPEG 2000 video, meaning a sequence of JPEG 2000 images, inside RTP packets. The payload format is designed to take advantage of JPEG 2000 features such as scalability. This is a Proposed Standard, extended by RFC 5372.

eli5.summary: A video is a flip book of pictures. This memo says how to cut each picture into pieces that fit into small mail packets, so they can be sent over the Internet and put back together.

questions: how to stream jpeg 2000 video over rtp
what is the rtp payload format for jpeg 2000
how is jpeg 2000 fragmented in rtp
what is the jpeg 2000 rtp payload header
subtitle: How to chop JPEG 2000 video frames into RTP packets and describe them in SDP.

tldr.problem: JPEG 2000 is a scalable image compression standard, and Motion JPEG 2000 defines a file format, not a way to send a series of images over a network.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries an 8-byte payload header (scan type, main header flag, tile number, fragment offset and more) followed by pieces of a JPEG 2000 codestream. The RFC also registers the video/jpeg2000 media type and its SDP parameters.
tldr.outcome: Video is sent as a continuous series of independently compressed JPEG 2000 images. RFC 5372 adds extensions for scalability and main header recovery.

today: RFC 5371 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is extended by RFC 5372, which covers scalability and main header recovery.

sections.title: Sending JPEG 2000 Video over RTP
sections.content:
This RFC specifies a payload format for JPEG 2000 video streams over the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). JPEG 2000 is ISO/IEC 15444-1 and ITU-T Rec. T.800, a still-image compression standard. Part 3, Motion JPEG 2000, defines a file format, not a transmission format, so this document supplies a network transmission format for a series of JPEG 2000 images.

The RFC lists features JPEG 2000 has over the older JPEG standard: higher compression efficiency with less visual distortion at extreme ratios, one codestream offering both lossy and lossless compression, better error resiliency, progressive transmission by pixel accuracy and by resolution, and random codestream access.

A JPEG 2000 video stream is a continuous series of still images. Each frame is compressed independently (a full intra-frame format), which gives low encoding and decoding delay. The RFC also notes that JPEG 2000 has flexible rate control suited to traffic and congestion control.
sections.eli5: A movie is just many photos shown one after another. Each photo here is squeezed on its own, so you never need the previous photo to open the next one.

sections.title: How a JPEG 2000 Codestream Is Built
sections.content:
The encoder transforms the image into wavelet coefficients, quantizes them, then forms code blocks inside precincts inside tiles. Each code block is coded with EBCOT and arithmetically encoded by bit plane, and rate control aims for the best quality at a given rate. The resulting data units, called JPEG 2000 packets, are interleaved along four axes: layer, resolution, component and precinct.

The finished codestream starts with a main header that begins with the SOC marker, then holds one or more tiles, and ends with the EOC marker. Each tile has a tile-part header that starts with SOT and ends with SOD, followed by a bitstream of JPEG 2000 packets.

The RFC does not describe the coding procedure in detail and points readers to JPEG 2000 texts.
sections.eli5: The picture is cut into little tiles and squeezed. All the pieces are stacked in a file with a start mark at the front and an end mark at the back.

sections.title: Payload Design Goals
sections.content:
The design takes packet loss into account. The RFC says 5% packet loss is common on the Internet and can reach 20% or more, so the codestream has to be split into RTP packets in a way that limits decoding trouble from missing ones. If the main header is lost, the image cannot be decoded.

The payload header carries markers that exploit JPEG 2000 scalability: markers for headers and header fragments, tile numbering to associate packets, interlace odd/even field markers, a priority field, and main header recovery information. The priority and recovery methods are described in RFC 5372.
sections.eli5: Mail sometimes gets lost, so every piece is labeled with what it is and where it goes, and the most important pieces are easy to spot.

sections.title: The RTP Payload Header
sections.content:
Each RTP packet has the normal RTP fixed header, then an 8-byte JPEG 2000 payload header, then the payload, which is a piece of a codestream and usually a JPEG 2000 packet. The payload header fields are:

  • tp (2 bits): scan type. 0 is progressive, 1 is part of an odd field of an interlaced frame, 2 is part of an even field.
  • MHF (2 bits): main header flag. 0 means no main header, 1 a piece of a fragmented header, 2 the last part of a fragmented header, 3 a whole main header.
  • mh_id (3 bits): used for main header recovery. Implementations following only this RFC SHOULD set it to 0 and receivers SHOULD ignore it.
  • T (1 bit): set to 1 when the tile number is invalid, which happens when a packet holds only the main header or when multiple tile-parts are packed together; otherwise 0.
  • priority (8 bits): importance of the packet. Senders following only this RFC SHOULD set it to 255 and receivers SHOULD ignore it.
  • tile number (16 bits): valid only when T is 0.
  • Reserved (8 bits): senders MUST set it to 0 and receivers MUST ignore it.
  • fragment offset (24 bits): the byte offset of this payload from the start of the codestream. It is counted from the first byte of the same frame even across multiple RTP sessions, so it might not start from 0 in some sessions.
sections.eli5: Every piece of the picture gets a small tag saying whether it is a whole or half-page, which tile it is, and how far into the picture it starts.

sections.title: RTP Fixed Header Usage
sections.content:
The marker bit MUST be 1 for the last RTP packet of a video frame and 0 otherwise. When several RTP sessions are used, it is 1 in the last packet of the frame in each session.

The payload type is dynamically assigned by means outside the RFC, such as RTSP or SIP signaling.

The timestamp is the presentation time of the frame, and every RTP packet carrying a fragment of a frame MUST have the same value. For interlaced video, the odd field and its matching even field MUST have the same timestamp. Senders and receivers MUST support the 90kHz timestamp rate and MAY support others. Rates below 1000 Hz SHOULD NOT be used, because they give too little resolution for RTCP measurements such as interarrival jitter. The clock rate MUST be negotiated at session start and, in SDP, expressed with rtpmap. If a non-90kHz rate is used, the RFC RECOMMENDS also offering 90kHz under a different payload type.
sections.eli5: All the pieces of one picture carry the same time stamp, and the last piece has a flag raised so the receiver knows the picture is complete.

sections.title: Packetization Rules
sections.content:
A packetization unit is a JPEG 2000 main header, a tile-part header, or a JPEG 2000 packet. The sender divides the codestream into these units and packs them into RTP packets. It can put any number of units into one packet, but MUST preserve codestream order.

If a unit plus the IP, RTP and payload headers is larger than the MTU, the unit MAY be fragmented. A fragmented unit MUST NOT share an RTP packet with the following unit.
sections.eli5: You can put several small pieces in one envelope, in order. A piece too big for an envelope gets split, and the split parts get envelopes to themselves.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type video/jpeg2000. The required parameters are rate, the RTP timestamp clock rate with a default of 90000, and sampling, the color space: RGB, BGR, RGBA, BGRA, YCbCr-4:4:4, YCbCr-4:2:2, YCbCr-4:2:0, YCbCr-4:1:1, GRAYSCALE, or a registered extension value. Optional parameters are interlace (1 for interlaced, otherwise 0), and width and height, which must both appear if either does. Receivers MUST ignore unspecified parameters. The type is defined only for transfer via RTP.

In SDP, the media name MUST be video, the encoding name in a=rtpmap MUST be jpeg2000, and the parameters go in a=fmtp. With offer/answer, sampling MUST appear in the offer and, if accepted, in the answer. Receivers that cannot handle the offered color space or interlace setting should reply with their preferred setting and end the session gracefully. Width and height in an offer are the maximum the sender can offer, and in an answer SHOULD be the maximum the receiver can accommodate. In multicast, the sender should accommodate the lowest values it receives from all answers.
sections.eli5: Before sending, the two sides swap a short note saying what colors, picture size and clock they can handle. If the receiver cannot cope, it says what it prefers.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification (RFC 3550) and any RTP profile. The main concerns are confidentiality, integrity and source authenticity. The RFC says no single mechanism fits every case; it recommends SRTP (RFC 3711) if suitable, and names IPsec and TLS (for RTP over TCP) as other options.

For congestion control, if a QoS-enhanced service is used, receivers SHOULD monitor packet loss to check the requested service is delivered. For best-effort service, users MUST monitor packet loss. Loss is acceptable if a TCP flow on the same path under the same conditions would achieve average throughput not less than the RTP flow. This can be met by adapting the transmission rate or the number of subscribed layers, or by having a receiver leave the session if loss is too high.
sections.eli5: Video can be protected with locks so nobody can peek or tamper. Senders should also slow down if the network is jammed, so they do not squeeze out others.

fields.desc: Scan type: 0 progressive, 1 odd field, 2 even field.

fields.name: MHF
fields.desc: Main header flag: 0 none, 1 piece, 2 last part, 3 whole header.

fields.name: mh_id
fields.desc: Main header identification, used for header recovery.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: 1 when the tile number is invalid.

fields.name: tile number
fields.desc: Tile number of the payload, valid when T is 0.

fields.desc: Byte offset from the start of the codestream.
